query: The Co-free FeNiCrMn system was selected to reduce cost while retaining the mechanical performance of equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi; prior work reported comparable or better mechanical properties after excluding Co. Research on FeNiCrMn has mainly addressed corrosion, while studies of related high- and medium-entropy alloys examined dynamic responses under tension or compression, different temperatures and strain rates, compositional changes, and the presence of cracks or voids. Those studies established that dynamic properties are sensitive to loading regime and material condition, but their different chemistries and defect states do not identify what governs FeNiCrMn. Under the constraints of retaining the Co-free composition and its strength–ductility balance, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis explains the dynamic behavior of solidified FeNiCrMn across temperature and strain-rate regimes? Define a controlled study capable of testing the hypothesis, its applicable boundaries, the prior findings that support it, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In as‐solidified Co‐free FeNiCrMn, the dynamic strength–ductility balance across varied temperature and strain‐rate regimes is governed by a shift in the dominant deformation mechanism: with dislocation glide prevailing at high temperatures/low strain rates and deformation twinning becoming activated at low temperatures/high strain rates.
generation.material_initial_state: As‐solidified, homogeneous Co‐free FeNiCrMn alloy with an FCC-dominant microstructure, minimal pre-existing twins, and uniformly distributed lattice defects.
generation.intervention: Subject the alloy to uniaxial tensile (or compression) tests under controlled temperatures (e.g., cryogenic, room, and elevated temperatures) and a range of strain rates (from quasi‐static to dynamic loading).
generation.conditions: Testing across a matrix of temperatures (for example, 77 K, 300 K, and 500 K) combined with different strain rate conditions (from ~10−3 s−1 to ~10^3 s−1) while keeping sample composition and processing constant.
generation.structural_mediator: The nucleation and density of deformation twins versus dislocation structures within the microstructure.
generation.mechanism: At low temperatures and high strain rates, the alloy’s low stacking fault energy favors the nucleation of deformation twins (twinning-induced plasticity) which act as barriers to dislocation motion, thereby elevating yield strength and strain rate sensitivity. Conversely, at higher temperatures or lower strain rates, thermal activation facilitates dislocation glide and recovery processes, reducing twin formation and leading to more conventional plastic flow.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under high strain rate and low temperature conditions, mechanical testing and post-mortem microscopy (e.g., TEM) should reveal a significant increase in twin density correlating with increased yield strength and reduced ductility. At elevated temperatures and/or lower strain rates, the microstructure will exhibit primarily dislocation networks with lower twin densities, corresponding to reduced yield strength but improved ductility.
generation.baseline: The mechanical performance and deformation modes observed in equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi and similar high-entropy alloys, where deformation twinning is known to augment strength and strain rate sensitivity under dynamic loading.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to be dominant in the as-solidified Co-free FeNiCrMn alloy with an FCC-based structure; however, if processing variations or the presence of secondary phases (e.g., precipitates) arise, other mechanisms (such as dislocation pile-up or dynamic recovery) might play more significant roles. The hypothesis applies over the specified temperature (77 K–500 K) and strain rate (~10−3 s−1 to ~10^3 s−1) regimes.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative contributions of twinning versus dislocation slip to the overall mechanical response remain uncertain, and interaction with potential dynamic recovery processes at intermediate temperatures may introduce secondary effects not fully captured by this single mechanism hypothesis.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of as-solidified FeNiCrMn alloy samples and perform uniaxial tensile tests at multiple temperatures (e.g., 77 K, 300 K, 500 K) and strain rates (from 10−3 s−1 to 10^3 s−1). For each test, record the stress–strain behavior and use high-resolution electron microscopy (TEM or EBSD) to quantify and map the prevalence of deformation twins versus dislocation structures.
measurements: Yield strength and ultimate tensile strength
Strain rate sensitivity from stress–strain curves
Twin density and distribution via TEM or EBSD imaging
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if, across the range of temperatures and strain rates, there is no statistically significant increase in twin density correlated with increased yield strength and strain rate sensitivity under high strain rate/low temperature conditions, or if deformation twinning is observed to be negligible and dislocation glide remains the dominant mechanism regardless of the testing conditions.

Nanoindentation behavior of high entropy alloys with transformation-induced plasticity

Abstract: Nanoindentation of three metastable dual-phase high entropy alloys (HEAs) was performed to obtain their inherent elastoplastic deformation responses. Excellent combination of hardness and elastic modulus in as-cast condition confirmed that, their inherently higher strength compared to other HEAs reported in literature, can be attributed to alloy chemistry induced phase stability. Further, hardness of 8.28 GPa combined with modulus of 221.8 GPa was obtained in Fe-Mn-Co-Cr-Si-Cu HEA by annealing the as-cast material, which is the best hardness-modulus combination obtained to date in HEAs from nanoindentation. Tensile deformation behavior of twist grain boundaries in CoCrFeMnNi high entropy alloy bicrystals

Abstract: AbstractHigh entropy alloys (HEA) are a class of materials that consist of multiple elemental species in similar concentrations. The use of elements in far from dilute concentrations introduces a multi-dimensional composition design space by which the properties of metallic systems can be tailored. While the mechanical behavior of HEAs has been the subject of active research recently, the role of grain boundaries (GBs) in their deformation behavior remains poorly understood. Motivated by recent experiments on HEAs demonstrating that GBs act as nucleation sites for deformation twins, herein, we leverage atomistic simulations to construct a series of equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEA bicrystals with ⟨110⟩ and ⟨111⟩ symmetric twist GBs and examine their tensile behavior and underlying deformation mechanisms at 77 K. Simulation results reveal that plastic deformation proceeds by the nucleation of partial dislocations from GBs, which then grow with further loading by bowing into the bulk crystals leaving behind stacking faults. Temperature-Dependent Superplasticity and Strengthening in CoNiCrFeMn High Entropy Alloy Nanowires Using Atomistic Simulations

Abstract: High strength and ductility, often mutually exclusive properties of a structural material, are also responsible for damage tolerance. At low temperatures, due to high surface energy, single element metallic nanowires such as Ag usually transform into a more preferred phase via nucleation and propagation of partial dislocation through the nanowire, enabling superplasticity. In high entropy alloy (HEA) CoNiCrFeMn nanowires, the motion of the partial dislocation is hindered by the friction due to difference in the lattice parameter of the constituent atoms which is responsible for the hardening and lowering the ductility. In this study, we have examined the temperature-dependent superplasticity of single component Ag and multicomponent CoNiCrFeMn HEA nanowires using molecular dynamics simulations. The results demonstrate that Ag nanowires exhibit apparent temperature-dependent superplasticity at cryogenic temperature due to (110) to (100) cross-section reorientation behavior.
